nx_dose_001: Both strengths are decimals of a milligram - line up the decimal places (0.075 vs 0.025) before dividing, and expect a small whole-tablet answer.
nx_dose_002: Use desired dose over available strength. When the ordered dose is not a multiple of the tablet strength, a half-tablet answer is legitimate - do not force a whole number.
nx_dose_003: Desired over have: 7.5 mg ordered against 5 mg tablets. Sanity-check the result - a safe oral order is almost always between half a tablet and 3 tablets.
nx_dose_004: Confirm ordered dose and supplied strength share a unit, then divide desired by have. An answer above 3-4 tablets should make you re-check the arithmetic before selecting it.
nx_dose_005: Digoxin strengths are decimal milligrams - keep the trailing digits (0.25 vs 0.125) aligned when dividing, because a misplaced decimal here is a tenfold dosing error.
nx_dose_006: For liquids, the formula is desired over have TIMES the vehicle volume - keep the 'per 5 mL' attached to the strength instead of treating 250 mg as per-mL.
nx_dose_007: Set up desired/have x volume. Divide 480 by 160 first to get a clean multiplier, then apply the 5 mL - clean intermediate numbers are a sign the setup is right.
nx_dose_008: The label reads per 1 mL, so the vehicle multiplier is 1 - the trap is reflexively multiplying by 5 because most suspension labels use 5 mL.
nx_dose_009: Desired/have x volume: 250 over 125 doubles the 5 mL vehicle. Estimate before computing - the ordered dose is twice the labeled strength, so the volume must be twice the labeled volume.
nx_dose_010: Notice the ordered dose is SMALLER than the labeled strength, so the answer must be less than the 5 mL vehicle volume - if your setup gives more than 5 mL, the fraction is inverted.
nx_dose_011: The weight is already in kilograms - multiply mg/kg by kg directly. Only convert when the stem gives pounds; converting a weight that is already metric is the planted error.
nx_dose_012: Convert pounds to kilograms FIRST (divide by 2.2), then multiply by mg/kg. Skipping the conversion inflates the dose by a factor of 2.2 - a classic pediatric overdose trap.
nx_dose_013: Weight is in kg, so this is a single multiplication. Write the units out (mg/kg x kg) and confirm kilograms cancel, leaving milligrams.
nx_dose_014: 110 lb must become kilograms before anything else: divide by 2.2, then multiply by 15 mg/kg. If the answer looks like a 100+ kg adult dose, the conversion was skipped.
nx_dose_015: Small decimal doses (0.1 mg/kg) punish sloppy decimals - multiply 0.1 by the weight and place the decimal deliberately; morphine errors of one decimal place are tenfold errors.
nx_dose_016: mL/hr is total volume divided by total hours - nothing else. Ignore any urge to involve drop factors; those belong only to gravity-drip questions.
nx_dose_017: Divide total mL by total hours. When it does not divide evenly, follow the stem's rounding instruction rather than truncating.
nx_dose_018: Volume over time: 250 mL across 2 hours. Estimate first - the answer must be near half the bag per hour - and reject options far from the estimate.
nx_dose_019: Large-volume, long-duration orders still reduce to mL divided by hours; 1800 over 24 gives a clean rate. A rate above 200 mL/hr on a maintenance infusion should trigger a re-check.
nx_dose_020: The 20 mEq KCl is descriptive, not computational - additives never change a rate question, which is still volume divided by hours. Distractor data is placed to be used.
nx_dose_021: Gravity drip: mL x drop factor, divided by MINUTES. The stem already gives minutes - resist converting to hours, which is only needed when time is stated in hours.
nx_dose_022: Use (volume x drop factor) / minutes and round gtt/min to a whole number - you cannot count a fraction of a drop.
nx_dose_023: Time is given in minutes, so plug it straight into (mL x gtt factor) / min. Converting 240 minutes to 4 hours and then forgetting the x60 is the planted error.
nx_dose_024: With a 60 gtt/mL microdrip set over 60 minutes, gtt/min equals mL/hr numerically - use that identity as a built-in check on your arithmetic.
nx_dose_025: Short IVPB windows still use (volume x drop factor) / minutes; small numbers make estimation easy - approximate first, then compute, and the pick should match the estimate.
nx_dose_026: The order and the record use different units (mcg vs mg) - convert one to the other by moving the decimal three places BEFORE comparing, and only then judge equivalence.
nx_dose_027: Grams to milligrams means multiplying by 1000: 0.5 g is 500 mg. Write the conversion as its own step - unit errors here are thousandfold errors.
nx_dose_028: One household teaspoon is 5 mL. Convert the prescribed mL into teaspoons by dividing by 5, and remember household measures are approximations - which is why the stem asks for them explicitly.
nx_dose_029: Use the concentration printed AFTER reconstitution (mg per mL of the final solution). The volume of diluent you added is a distractor - it is not the denominator.
nx_dose_030: Desired dose over final concentration gives the injection volume. Check plausibility: parenteral volumes are usually a few mL, so a 20+ mL answer means a setup error.
nx_dose_031: Decimal concentrations (62.5 mg/mL) reward writing the division out fully; estimate the answer against the nearest round concentration (60) to confirm the magnitude.
nx_dose_032: Safe-dose questions are mg/kg/DAY - compute the daily maximum first, then divide by the number of doses per day. Comparing a per-dose order against the daily limit is the planted trap.
nx_dose_033: Anchor on the words 'per day divided every 6 hours': daily total first (mg/kg x kg), then split across 4 doses. Only after both steps can you judge whether one ordered dose is safe.
nx_dose_034: Work in two labeled steps - total daily maximum, then per-dose maximum at 4 doses/day. If you find yourself using 40 mg/kg as a per-dose number, you have skipped the division.
nx_dose_035: Infusion time is volume divided by rate. Keep the units visible (mL over mL/hr leaves hours) so the answer's unit confirms the setup.
nx_dose_036: Divide volume by rate for hours; when the result is fractional, convert the fraction of an hour into minutes by multiplying by 60 rather than reading 0.5 hr as 50 minutes.
nx_dose_037: Weight-based drips go stepwise: mcg/min (dose x kg), then mcg/hr (x60), then mL/hr (divide by the bag's mcg per mL). Compute the bag concentration first and label every intermediate unit.
nx_dose_038: With tiny doses (0.1 mcg/kg/min) the decimals do the damage - carry units through dose x weight x 60 / concentration and let the surviving unit (mL/hr) prove the chain was right.
nx_dose_039: Convert the bag to mcg/mL before anything else, then dose x kg x 60 over that concentration. Skipping the mg-to-mcg conversion on the bag is the thousandfold trap.
nx_dose_040: Heparin protocols are units/kg/HR - no x60 step, unlike mcg/kg/min drips. Multiply units/kg/hr by weight, then divide by the bag's units per mL.
nx_dose_041: Same protocol, different weight: the method must not change. Units/hr (18 x kg) divided by the bag concentration in units/mL - and a heavier client must yield a proportionally higher rate.
